core: Correlation as a relationship between variables: as one changes, the other tends to change too (a link)
Causation as a cause-and-effect claim: one thing makes another happen
Why people confuse them: the mind loves patterns and over-reads coincidences as causes (illusory correlation)
The third-variable (confounding variable) problem: a hidden factor may drive both observed variables
Reverse causation: the causal arrow may point the opposite way from the headline's story
Experiments as the method that can isolate cause (sibling topic: experiments)
Honest note: even good studies leave questions
Honest framing: correlation is a question, experiments are the answer
supporting: The correlation coefficient (r) as the statistic that measures strength and direction of a linear relationship
The distinction between correlational research (passive observation) and experimental research (manipulation)
Media misreporting of correlational evidence as causal evidence
outOfScope: The full mechanics of the correlation coefficient and scatterplot interpretation (sibling topic: correlation)
Experimental design details such as random assignment, control groups, and blinding (sibling topic: experiments)
The overall taxonomy of research methods (sibling topic: research-methods)

claims.claim: A correlation is a relationship between two variables: when they are correlated, as one variable changes, so does the other.
Causation is a cause-and-effect relationship: changes in one variable produce changes in another.
Correlational data cannot be used to make claims about cause-and-effect relationships.
A third (confounding) variable may be the actual cause of the systematic movement in both correlated variables of interest, creating the illusion of a direct link.
Correlation does not specify which variable is explanatory and which is the outcome, so the causal arrow may point in either direction (reverse causation).
People have a tendency to look for relationships between variables that do not really exist, which fuels mistaken causal conclusions.

Experiments, in which the researcher actively makes changes in one variable and watches for changes in another, allow researchers to make causal inferences; the only way to claim a relationship is cause and effect is to perform an experiment.
The correlation coefficient (r) takes values between -1 and 1 and describes the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables.

Experiments are often conducted in artificial settings, which raises questions about how findings apply in real-world settings, and many questions cannot be pursued experimentally because of ethical concerns.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The phrase 'correlation does not imply causation' is sometimes read as meaning correlational evidence is worthless, while in practice correlational research is a legitimate and widely used method.
positions: Correlational findings can never establish cause and effect (OpenStax 2.2; Noba Research Designs).
Correlational research remains valuable for identifying relationships and generating questions that experiments can then test (Noba Research Designs tradeoffs section).
Media coverage frequently represents correlational evidence as causal evidence, overstating what the studies show (Noba Research Designs).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents correlation as a genuine research tool that describes links and raises questions, while causation requires a different method (experiments); correlational evidence being non-causal does not make it worthless.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft described the topic in generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept in Psychology', 'a concept students use to organize information') with no factual content; no such claims were carried forward.
The draft's vocabulary definition for the topic term ('A foundational Psychology concept covered in this lesson') was circular and was replaced with verified definitions.

sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Tier A anchor. Supports: correlation measures the association between two variables (how they go together) in passive observation; experiments actively change one variable and watch for changes in another; experiments allow researchers to make causal inferences; a third variable (e.g., wealth) can cause both correlated variables and create the illusion of a direct link; 'correlation does not mean causation' is a repeated phrase among psychologists; correlational evidence is often incorrectly represented as causal evidence in media. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
